title.en: The lord of thieves, and the archers at every act

summary: Seventeen yajus, each opening and closing with namaḥ. The first eight salute Rudra as the lord of thieves and robbers of every kind — the secret and the open, the prowler in the house and in the market, the night-roamer and the land-seizer; the last nine, now addressed as ‘you’ (vaḥ), salute the archers at each act of shooting, then those who sit and lie, sleep and wake, stand and run, and the assemblies and the horses with their lords. Sāyaṇa explains the thieves: Rudra, like an actor, takes on every guise in play, or, as the self of all, is present in each as the Lord, whom the word ‘thief’ only points to, as one shows the moon at the tip of a branch.

vyakarana.note: √sah, ‘to overcome, prevail’, present participle middle (-māna), dative singular.
ni-vyādhin, from ni + √vyadh, ‘to pierce’, with the agent suffix -in; dative singular. Compare vivyādhin in the second anuvāka.

Feminine of ā-vyādhin (ā + √vyadh, ‘to strike at’), genitive plural, dependent on pataye: ‘the lord of the [women or bands] who attack’. Monier-Williams gives the plural as ‘a band of robbers’. Like pataye in the second anuvāka, pati with a genitive keeps the ordinary dative (P. 1.4.9).

translation.literal: Homage to the overpowering one, to the piercing one; to the lord of the assailing [bands] homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the victorious one who pierces; homage to the lord of the bands that attack.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa opens the anuvāka by saying that the second anuvāka gave some of the yajus with namaskāra on both sides, and that the third now gives more of the same kind, twelve of them not plain in meaning («तृतीयेऽस्पष्टार्थानि द्वादश यजूंष्य् उच्यन्ते»). His comment on this first yajus is not in the transcription of the bhāṣya used here, which passes from that introduction straight to the second yajus («अथ द्वितीयं यजुराह»).

flags.note: No comment of Sāyaṇa on this yajus survives in the witness (sayana.json, N3); the word meanings rest on the grammar and Monier-Williams. āvyādhinī is a rare word (Monier-Williams: f. pl. ‘a band of robbers’).

vyakarana.note: kakubha, ‘lofty, excelling’, related to kakubh, ‘peak, summit’; dative singular.
niṣaṅga (ni + √sañj, ‘to hang on’: what hangs at one’s side, a quiver or a sword) + the possessive suffix -in; n → ṇ after ṣ in the same word (P. 8.4.2). Dative singular.

translation.literal: Homage to the eminent one, to the one with a sword; to the lord of thieves homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the chief who bears a sword; homage to the lord of thieves.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: kakubha means like a peak, that is, chief («ककुभ-सदृशाय प्रधानभूतायेत्यर्थः»); the niṣaṅgin has a sword in his hand; the stena are thieves who steal in secret («स्तेना गुप्तचोराः»), and homage is to their protector. He then explains why Rudra is hailed as the lord of thieves. Rudra in play takes on this guise and that, like an actor («रुद्रो हि लीलया नट इव तत्तद्वेषं धत्ते»); or, since he is the self of the whole world, he is present in whatever form beings take, and the mantras speak so that one may contemplate Rudra as the self of all («रुद्रस्य सार्वात्म्यमनुसंधातुं»). In the bodies of thieves and the like Rudra is present in two ways, as the individual self and as the Lord («जीवरूपेणेश्वररूपेण च»). The individual self is what words like ‘thief’ denote, and it is what the śāstras censure; the Lord is only indicated by them («स्तेनादिशब्दैरुपलक्ष्यते»), and contemplating him is the highest human end, because it destroys sin («पापक्षय-हेतुत्वेन परमपुरुषार्थ»). The common word points to the intended sense as one shows the moon ‘at the tip of the branch’ («यथा शाखाग्रे चन्द्र इत्यत्र»).
units.reflection: The litany does not leave out the thief. To bow even there is to look past what a person does to what is present in him.

flags.note: niṣaṅgin: Monier-Williams ‘having a quiver (or sword?)’. Sāyaṇa glosses it here as ‘sword in hand’ and in the next yajus takes niṣaṅga as the arrow held in the hand. The translation follows him in each place.

samasa.vigraha: इषवः धीयन्ते अस्मिन्निति इषुधिः; इषुधिः अस्य अस्तीति इषुधिमान्
samasa.meaning: having a quiver (iṣudhi, ‘that in which arrows are placed’, from √dhā)

vyakarana.note: iṣudhi, ‘quiver’ (iṣu ‘arrow’ + -dhi from √dhā, ‘to place’), + the possessive suffix -mat; dative singular -mate.
Genitive plural of taskara, ‘robber’; n → ṇ after r (P. 8.4.2).

translation.literal: Homage to the one who holds the arrow, to the one who has a quiver; to the lord of robbers homage.
translation.readable: Homage to him who holds an arrow in his hand and a quiver on his back; homage to the lord of robbers.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: here the niṣaṅga is the arrow held in the hand to be fitted to the bow, and the iṣudhi the arrow-holder tied on the back («बाणाधार इषुधिः»); homage is to the one who has both («तदुभययुक्ताय नमः»). The taskara are thieves who rob openly («प्रकटचोराः»), in contrast with the secret stena of the previous yajus; homage is to their protector. Sāyaṇa’s explanation of why Rudra is saluted in the guise of thieves (given on the second yajus) applies here too.

flags.note: corrections.json, N3.3: W2 reads एषुधिमते; classified as a W2 error. The stem is iṣudhi- ‘quiver’ (Namakam 1.15, Namakam 7), and the text keeps इषुधिमते.
niṣaṅgin is glossed by Sāyaṇa as ‘sword in hand’ in yajus 2 and as ‘holding the arrow in the hand’ here; Monier-Williams ‘having a quiver (or sword?)’.

Genitive plural of the u-stem stāyu, ‘thief’ (= tāyu).

translation.literal: Homage to the one who goes slyly, to the one who sneaks about; to the lord of thieves homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the sly one who prowls around; homage to the lord of thieves.

vyakarana.note: niceru, a Vedic derivative of ni-√car, ‘to move about (low, stealthily)’; u-stem, dative singular -ave.
pari-cara, ‘moving about’, from pari-√car with the suffix -a; dative singular.
araṇya, ‘forest’, is a neuter noun; Sāyaṇa takes the word here as the forest thieves themselves («चोरा अरण्याः»), a masculine. The ā of the text (परिचरायारण्यानाम्) is paricarāya + araṇyānām.

translation.literal: Homage to the one who creeps, to the one who roams about; to the lord of the forest [robbers] homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the one who creeps about the house and the one who roams the streets; homage to the lord of the forest robbers.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: the niceru is one who keeps moving about, watchful, in his master’s own house, thinking when he will steal («स्वामिगृह एव कदाऽपहरिष्यामीत्यनया बुद्ध्या»); the paricara roams about the markets, streets and the like with intent to steal («आपणवीथिप्रवाटिकादावपहारबुद्ध्या चरणशीलः»); homage is to the one who is both («तदुभयरूपाय नमः»). The araṇya are thieves who live always in the forest and harm travellers by robbing them («निरन्तरमरण्ये वर्तमानाश्चोरा अरण्याः»), and homage is to their protector.

flags.note: araṇyānām may be read as the genitive of the neuter araṇya, ‘of the forests’; Sāyaṇa takes it as the forest-dwelling thieves. The translation follows Sāyaṇa.

vyakarana.note: Dative plural of sṛkāvin. Monier-Williams gives sṛka as ‘arrow, spear’ and sṛkāvin (also sṛkāyin) as ‘having an arrow or spear’, a possessive formation; Sāyaṇa takes the second part from √av, ‘to protect’ (compare ātatāvin in the second anuvāka).

Desiderative of √han, ‘to kill’: reduplicated ji-, h → gh, the nasal as anusvāra, -sa- (jighāṃsa-, ‘wish to kill’); present participle jighāṃsat, dative plural with t → d before bh. The text writes the Taittirīya ँ (जिघाँसद्भ्यः); the padaccheda uses anusvāra.
√muṣ, ‘to steal’ (9th class, muṣṇāti), present participle muṣṇat, genitive plural, dependent on pataye.

translation.literal: Homage to those who protect themselves with the spear, to those who wish to kill; to the lord of the robbers homage.
translation.readable: Homage to those armed with the spear and bent on killing; homage to the lord of those who steal.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «सृकशब्दो वज्रवाची» — the word sṛka denotes the vajra — and the sṛkāvin are those who protect their own bodies with it; the jighāṃsat are thieves who want to kill living beings («प्राणिनो हन्तुमिच्छन्तश्चोरा जिघांसन्तः»); homage is to the one who is both. The muṣṇat are those who, being cultivators («कृषिकाः सन्तः»), carry off their masters’ grain, and homage is to their protector.

flags.note: sṛka: Monier-Williams ‘arrow, spear’, and sṛkāvin ‘having an arrow or spear’; Sāyaṇa takes sṛka as the vajra and sṛkāvin as ‘protecting oneself with it’. The translation follows Sāyaṇa’s ‘protect’ with the dictionary’s ‘spear’; the word table gives both.

Adverbial accusative of nakta, ‘night’: ‘by night’. It is taken as a separate word, not as the first member of a compound naktaṃcara-: in W1 both naktam and caradbhyaḥ carry their own udātta (न and ञ्च are unmarked, क्त॒ marked anudātta before the second), and Sāyaṇa paraphrases with two words, «नक्तं चरन्तः». The m becomes ñ before c.
prakṛnta, from pra-√kṛt, ‘to cut up’ (present stem kṛnta-); Monier-Williams ‘one who cuts to pieces’ (with a variant vikṛnta in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā). Genitive plural.

translation.literal: Homage to the sword-bearers, to those who roam by night; to the lord of those who cut [people] down homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the sword-bearers who roam by night; homage to the lord of those who kill and rob.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: «असिमन्तः खड्गधारिणश्चोराः» — the asimat are thieves who carry swords — and those who go about at night and harm the people who have come out into the streets are the «नक्तं चरन्तः»; homage is to the one who is both («तदुभयरूपाय नमः»). The prakṛnta are those who kill first and then rob («हत्वैवापहरन्तः प्रकृन्ताः»), and homage is to their protector.

flags.note: corrections.json, N3.7: W2 reads ञक्त- for नक्त-; classified as a W2 error (naktam ‘by night’ + carat-; ñ cannot open the word).

W1 marks the last syllable of asimadbhyaḥ anudātta (असि॒मद्भ्यो॒), the mark before an udātta: naktam carries its own accent and stands as a word. W2 marks it svarita (असि॒मद्भ्यो॑ ञक्तं॒ चर॑द्भ्यः), which leaves the first syllable of naktam unaccented, as it would be in a compound naktaṃ-carat. The text and the padaccheda follow W1, with Sāyaṇa («नक्तं चरन्तः»).

those who pluck away the earth, seizers of land (Sāyaṇa’s analysis: ku, ‘earth’, + √luñc, ‘to pluck’)

vyakarana.note: uṣṇīṣa, ‘turban’, + the possessive suffix -in; n → ṇ after ṣ (P. 8.4.2). Dative singular.
√luñc, ‘to pluck, tear out’. Sāyaṇa takes ku as ‘earth’; Monier-Williams lists the word under the pejorative prefix ku- with the sense ‘one who plucks out hairs’ (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā).

translation.literal: Homage to the turbaned one, to the one who roams the mountains; to the lord of the seizers of land homage.
translation.readable: Homage to the turbaned one who roams the hills; homage to the lord of those who seize land.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: the uṣṇīṣin is one who has a head-wrap («शिरोवेष्टनवानुष्णीषी»), a thief who wraps his head with a turban like the village folk and moves among them («ग्राम्यजनवदुष्णीषेण शिरो वेष्टयित्वा»); the giricara goes about on the hill to rob those who gather wood («गिरौ काष्ठादिसंपादकानां») of their clothes and goods; homage is to the one who is both. The kuluñca are those who carry off the earth, ku, in the form of houses, fields and the like («कुं भूमिं», «लुञ्चन्त्य् अपहरन्तीति कुलुञ्चाः»), and homage is to their protector.

flags.note: kuluñca: Monier-Williams ‘one who plucks out hairs’ (ku- pejorative); Sāyaṇa ‘one who seizes land’ (ku = earth). The translation follows Sāyaṇa; the word table gives both.

A possessive formation in -āvin from dhanvan, ‘bow’ (Monier-Williams: dhanvāvin or dhanvāyin, ‘carrying a bow’); dative plural. Sāyaṇa glosses the word without analysing it.

From here to the end of the anuvāka the beings are addressed directly: vaḥ, the enclitic dative plural of yuṣmad (for yuṣmabhyam, P. 8.1.21), ‘to you’ (Sāyaṇa: «हे रुद्रा वो युष्मभ्यं नम»). The datives stand in apposition to it.

translation.literal: Homage [to you] the arrow-bearers, and to you the bow-bearers homage.
translation.readable: Homage to you who bear arrows, and to you who bear bows, homage.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: the iṣumat hold arrows in the hand to frighten («भीषयितुं हस्ते बाणधारिण इषुमन्तः»), and the dhanvāvin likewise hold bows («धनुर्धारिणो धन्वाविनः»); they are addressed as Rudras in both forms: «तदुभयरूपा हे रुद्रा वो युष्मभ्यं नम». The namaskāra is said twice so that the two qualifiers divide the sentence («विशेषणद्वयेन वाक्यं भेत्तुं द्विर्नमस्कारः»).

translation.readable: Homage to you who shoot, and to you who pierce, homage.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa distinguishes the two acts: asana is the carrying of the released arrow up to the target («मुक्तस्य बाणस्य लक्ष्यपर्यन्तं»), and those who do it are the asyat; vedha is the entry into the target of the arrow that has come near it («लक्ष्यसमीपं गतस्य बाणस्य लक्ष्ये प्रवेशो वेधः»), and those who do it are the vidhyat.
